answers.question: How does an O3 frontend module declare its configuration schema so implementers can override its settings? Point to the documentation and implementation.

paragraphs.text: An O3 frontend module declares configurable settings in a `config-schema.ts` file, registers it with `defineConfigSchema()` in `startupApp()`, and implementers override the resulting keys via a JSON config file.

**The pattern (docs)**
- Each module puts its configurable properties in `src/config-schema.ts` [1].
- The schema is registered in `startupApp()` using `defineConfigSchema(moduleName, configSchema)` [2].
- Full developer guide covering keywords (`_type`, `_default`, `_description`, `_validators`, `_elements`) and typing: [3].
- Module layout and the role of `config-schema.ts`: [4]. Canonical file layout list also at [5].

**Schema shape**
- Each config element is an object whose value carries schema keywords; `_type` uses the `Type` enum, all values need a `_default` [6].
- Real example: `@openmrs/esm-login-app` [7], including nested objects, array-of-object via `_elements` [8], and custom cross-field validators [9].

**Registration (implementation)**
- `startupApp()` calls `defineConfigSchema(moduleName, configSchema)` [10].
- `defineConfigSchema()` validates the schema, merges in the implicit schema, and stores it under the module name [11].
- `validateConfigSchema()` logs errors for reserved keys (`Display conditions`, `Translation overrides`), missing defaults, bad `_type`, and bad `_elements` [12].
- Every module implicitly gets the reserved keys, so modules need not declare them packages/framework/esm-config/src/module-config/module-config.ts.
- Extensions can have their own separate schema via `defineExtensionConfigSchema()` packages/framework/esm-config/src/module-config/module-config.ts.

**How implementer settings get applied**
- Implementers point the SPA at a JSON config file via `configUrls`; each key is a module name and its value overrides the schema-defined properties content/en-US/docs/configure-o3/overview.mdx.
- At runtime the config is merged per module, validated against the schema, and defaults are applied packages/framework/esm-config/src/module-config/module-config.ts.
- Config can also be supplied programmatically with `provide()` packages/framework/esm-config/src/module-config/module-config.ts, and read with `getConfig()` packages/framework/esm-config/src/module-config/module-config.ts.

```mermaid
---
title: Config schema to implementer override
---
flowchart TD
    schema["config-schema.ts"] --> startup["startupApp()"]
    startup --> define["defineConfigSchema()"]
    define --> validate["validateConfigSchema()"]
    validate --> store["configInternalStore"]
    implicit["implicit schema"] --> define
    store --> merge["merge implementer config"]
    json["implementer JSON config file"] --> merge
    merge --> defaults["setDefaults + validators"]
    defaults --> use["useConfig() in components"]
```

code: Per-app configuration is available in O3 via the built-in [configuration system](/docs/configuration-system). Each frontend module can define its own configuration schema in a `config-schema.ts` file inside its `src` directory. The following snippet is drawn from the Programs frontend module's config-schema:
'Whether to show the Program status field in the Record program enrollment and Edit program enrollment forms. If set to true, the `Program status` field is displayed in the Programs datatable',

The properties specified in the config schema allow implementers to tailor the behavior of the module to their needs. The configuration system also allows implementers to specify default values for the various configuration properties.
In Core v5+ modules, config schemas should be registered in the `startupApp()` function:
This ensures the schema is registered before the module's components are rendered.

**For implementers**: To learn how to configure your O3 instance, see the [Configure O3](/docs/configure-o3/overview) guide, which covers practical configuration tasks like branding, translations, and module-specific settings.
### How to make a frontend module configurable
You should use the OpenMRS Frontend Framework to make modules configurable.
The main task is to create a config schema for your module. The config schema is what tells the framework what configuration files should look like, including defaults and validations.

**Note**: Configuration schemas are optional. If your module doesn't need any configuration options (for example, if it's a library module like the [React Form Engine](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-esm-form-engine-lib) that receives all its configuration through props or function parameters), you don't need to define a schema. The configuration system will still work; modules without schemas use the implicit schema for `Display conditions` and `Translation overrides`.

You’ll probably start with some idea of what you want configs for your module to look like. Try and put yourself in the implementer’s shoes and imagine what features they will expect to be configurable, and what they might expect the configuration property to be called. Assume they don’t know anything about the internal workings of your module.

By way of example, let’s say we’re building a module for a virtual provider functionality at a very futuristic hospital. Maybe we want an implementer to be able to write the following in their config file:

We’ll start with just that first nested config element from above, `hologram.color`. We must provide defaults for all of the values—in OpenMRS Frontend 3.0, all configuration is optional. All modules should do something reasonable out of the box.

- It also exports two named lifecycle functions, `root` and `activePrescriptionsSummary`. These names must match the component names declared in `routes.json`. The app shell calls them when the corresponding page or extension needs to render.

- It also exports a `startupApp` function which is used to set up the frontend module. In this case, the frontend module's configuration schema is defined here. Modules that need breadcrumbs or other framework registration can do that in `startupApp` too.

Many frontend modules define a function named `startupApp`. This function performs setup that should happen once, immediately before the module's first page, extension, modal, or workspace lifecycle is loaded. The `startupApp` function is where we commonly:
- run other load-time setup that must happen before the module's exported lifecycles are used
Page and extension registration itself comes from `routes.json`, not from `startupApp`. If a module does not need load-time setup, `startupApp` can be omitted.
- `src/index.ts` - entry point that exports lifecycle functions and setup code
- `src/routes.json` - static route metadata for the app shell
- `src/config-schema.ts` - where the module’s configuration properties live
Frontend module code is loaded on demand by the app shell when it’s needed, which improves initial load performance.
